title: Tetris Challenge: College Programming Contest
description: While I was in college, a group of friends challenged each other to see who could build the best Tetris game. I built a Mario-themed DOS version in Turbo C++ with custom graphics, animated block skins, scoring, levels, line clearing, next-piece preview, and my own low-level VGA rendering pipeline. My entry won the challenge.

sections.title: Informal College Programming Challenge
paragraphs: A group of friends in college challenged each other to build the best Tetris game.
I created this version as my entry and won the challenge.

sections.title: Mario-Themed Tetris
paragraphs: I wrapped standard Tetris mechanics in a custom Mario-themed presentation.
The different block graphics were animated visual skins rather than different gameplay pieces.

sections.title: Core Tetris Systems
paragraphs: I implemented the game logic directly rather than using an existing game framework.

sections.title: DOS VGA Rendering
paragraphs: The game rendered in VGA Mode 13h at 320 x 200 with 256 colors.
Rather than relying on slow high-level graphics calls for every sprite and pixel, I rendered frames into an off-screen software buffer and copied the completed frame directly into VGA video memory.

sections.title: Software Double Buffering
paragraphs: The rendering system used a 64,000-byte back buffer corresponding to the full 320 x 200 Mode 13h framebuffer.
Game graphics were drawn into normal memory first, then the completed frame was copied to VGA memory in one operation.

sections.title: From Roughly 1 FPS to Real-Time Rendering
paragraphs: This project came from a period when I was learning why straightforward DOS graphics APIs were too slow for sprite-heavy games.

Learning to render into an off-screen framebuffer and copy the finished image directly to video memory transformed the kind of games I could build, taking my earlier graphics experiments from roughly 1 FPS into the range of smooth real-time animation.

sections.title: Direct VGA Memory
paragraphs: The surviving code writes completed frames directly to VGA memory rather than drawing the full game through BIOS graphics services.
It also includes vertical-retrace synchronization and direct palette manipulation.

sections.title: Custom Graphics Utilities
paragraphs: I built reusable low-level graphics routines around the DOS framebuffer.

sections.title: 8-bit Bitmap Pipeline
paragraphs: The game loads 8-bit BMP graphics and palette data for sprites, tiles, and presentation assets.
This let me build a custom sprite-based interface while still working within the 256-color VGA environment.

sections.title: Animated Presentation
paragraphs: The presentation included animated Mario-themed elements, background animation, stars, custom block artwork, and a custom title screen rather than using a plain Tetris board.

sections.title: Artwork
paragraphs: I drew the Mario and Luigi characters, the title-screen presentation, and some of the tile graphics myself.
Some tile graphics were adapted from existing Mario game artwork.

sections.title: No Audio
paragraphs: This version did not include sound or music.

sections.title: Low-Level Graphics Learning
paragraphs: This project represents an important stage in my transition from using built-in DOS graphics routines toward writing my own real-time rendering infrastructure.
The same period included separate experiments with assembly and BIOS interrupts, but the surviving Tetris implementation itself is primarily Turbo C++ with direct framebuffer and VGA-memory access.

historicalNotes: The legacy portfolio card was titled 'Tetris Challenge (1997)'.
This was an informal programming challenge between Jamie and college friends, not an official institutional competition.
Jamie remembers his entry winning the challenge.
The surviving source is Turbo C++ / DOS-era code.
The surviving code explicitly switches to VGA Mode 13h, 320 x 200, 256 colors.
The source uses a 64,000-byte software back buffer and copies the completed frame into VGA video memory.
Jamie's historical term 'Shadow RAM' appears to refer to the off-screen software framebuffer/back-buffer technique taught in college.
For modern public terminology, use 'software double buffering', 'off-screen framebuffer', or 'back buffer' rather than relying on the ambiguous term 'Shadow RAM'.
The old portfolio card listed Assembly, but no convincing assembly implementation survives in the current Tetris source and Jamie does not remember using assembly in the finished game.
Remove Assembly from the public Tetris technology list.
Jamie did separately experiment with assembly and BIOS interrupts during the same learning period.
Jamie remembers attempting sprite graphics using interrupt-driven approaches before learning the framebuffer technique and finding the interrupt-based approach too slow.

The surviving Tetris source contains low-level DOS graphics code including BIOS mode switching, direct VGA memory access, palette I/O, back-buffer copying, bitmap loading, drawing primitives, and vertical-retrace handling.
Some unrelated RPG/game-development code is mixed into the surviving source folder and should not automatically be attributed to the finished Tetris game.
Jamie drew the Mario and Luigi characters, title-screen presentation, and some tile artwork.
Some tile graphics were adapted from existing Mario game assets.
The Mario-themed block graphics were cosmetic/animated skins; standard Tetris gameplay remained underneath.
There was no sound or music.

The approximate improvement from roughly 1 FPS to around 30 FPS belongs to Jamie's broader contemporary graphics-learning recollection and should not be presented as a benchmark measured specifically from the surviving Tetris build unless stronger evidence is recovered.
